Variance of documented NFRs

Julian Frattini

2026-04-20

This notebook contains the analysis of the variance of responses to the options available for the question “Which classes of non-functional requirements do you explicitly consider in your requirements documentation?” across demographic factors. The following options were available to select for this question:

Code Name Text
v_97 Compatibility Compatibility (e.g., co-existence, interoperability)
v_98 Maintainability Maintainability (e.g., analysability, modularity, modifiability, reusability, testability)
v_99 Performance efficiency Performance efficiency (e.g., time behaviour, resource utilisation, capacity)
v_100 Portability Portability (e.g., adaptability, install ability, replaceability)
v_101 Reliability Reliability (e.g., availability, fault tolerance, maturity, recoverability)
v_102 Safety Safety (e.g. freedom of risk for health or distaster)
v_303 Security Security (e.g., accountability, authenticity, confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation)
v_103 Usability Usability (e.g., accessibility, appropriateness recognizability, learnability, operability, user error protection, user interface aesthetics)
v_422 Constraints External or internal constraints (e.g. laws)
v_104 Other Other (please specify)

For analysis, we follow the 3-step framework for statistical causal inference as summarized by Siebert.1

# short name of the question
q = "documented NFRs"
# list of variables representing the options for the question
v <- c("v_97", "v_98", "v_99", "v_100", "v_101", "v_102", "v_303", "v_103", 
       "v_422", "v_104")

# names of the options 
labels = c("Compatibility", "Maintainability", "Performance efficiency",
           "Portability", "Reliability", "Safety", "Security", "Usability",
           "Constraints", "Other")

# minimum likelihood of responses to be considered "common"
level.common <- 0.2

Variables

We consider the following demographic factors:

Code Name Question Type
v_23 country In which country are you personally located? categorical
v_3 size How many people are involved in your project? numeric
v_457 way of working How would you personally characterise the way your project works? ordinal
v_1 sector Please select the main industrial sector of your project or the application domain of the software you build. categorical
v_16 external Does your project involve external partners? binary
v_357 distributed Is your project distributed? binary
v_377 virtualization Do you tend to work from home, on-site, or both? ordinal
v_17 role What is the main role you occupy in your project? categorical

Data Analysis

We analyze the variance of the response variable following established practices of Bayesian data analysis.2

d <- load_data(run = "2024", data_path = "../../data", file = "runs/napire2024/data_cleaned_2024.csv") %>% 
  select(
    "lfdn", # respondent identifier
    "v_3", "Country", "v_1", "v_457", "v_16", "v_357", "v_377", "v_17", # demographic factors
    all_of(v) # response variables
    ) %>% 
  drop_na()

str(d)

##  $ lfdn   : int  100 102 104 106 108 109 111 115 117 119 ...
##  $ v_3    : int  20 5 8 20 25 25 7 20 6 5 ...
##  $ Country: chr  "Germany" "Sweden" "Germany" "Sweden" ...
##  $ v_1    : Factor w/ 22 levels "Agriculture",..: 5 2 6 12 6 15 2 10 17 17 ...
##  $ v_457  : Ord.factor w/ 6 levels "Agile"<"Rather agile"<..: 5 1 3 2 1 4 5 1 4 2 ...
##  $ v_16   : Factor w/ 3 levels "Yes","No","I don't know": 1 2 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 1 ...
##  $ v_357  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE ...
##  $ v_377  : Ord.factor w/ 6 levels "Almost completely on-site"<..: 3 1 3 2 1 5 3 4 3 2 ...
##  $ v_17   : Factor w/ 12 levels "Business Analyst",..: 12 3 4 11 5 8 4 1 3 11 ...
##  $ v_97   : logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...
##  $ v_98   : logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...
##  $ v_99   : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE ...
##  $ v_100  : logi  FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...
##  $ v_101  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE ...
##  $ v_102  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...
##  $ v_303  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE TRUE ...
##  $ v_103  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE ...
##  $ v_422  : logi  TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE ...
##  $ v_104  : logi  FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE ...

For each outcome variable, we train one Bayesian regression model on all demographic variables as predictors.

Modelling

First, we define a formula regressing the outcome variable of interest on the demographic factors

f <- 
  eval(parse(text = paste0("bf(mvbind(", 
                           paste(v, collapse = ", "),
                           ") ~ 1 + v_3 + Country + v_1 + v_457 + v_16 + v_357 + v_377 + v_17)",
                           "+ set_rescor(FALSE)")))

# get_prior(f, data = d, family = bernoulli())

For each coefficient implied by a predictor, we specify a prior based on domain knowledge.

p <- c(
  set_prior("normal(0, 1)", class = "Intercept", resp = gsub("_", "", v)), 
  set_prior("normal(0, 0.2)", class = "b", resp = gsub("_", "", v))
)

Since the response variables are all binary (yes/no), we model them using a multivariate Bernoulli distribution utilizing a logit link to map the linear model to the parameter space of \(p\).

m.prior <-
  brm(data = d, family = bernoulli, formula = f, prior = p,
    iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
    seed = 4, sample_prior="only",
    file = paste0("../fits/variance.", v[1], ".prior"), file_refit = "on_change"
  )

brms::pp_check(m.prior, ndraws=100, type = "bars", resp = gsub("_", "", v[1]))

The prior predictive check (for one of the response variable options) confirms the plausibility of the selected prior probability distribution. Given the number of predictors, the weight towards the extreme values is anticipated. Next, we update the coefficient distributions in light of the collected data using Monte Carlo Markov Chain sampling.

m <-
  brm(data = d, family = bernoulli, formula = f, prior = p,
    iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 4, 
    file = paste0("../fits/variance.", v[1]), file_refit = "on_change"
  )

brms::pp_check(m, ndraws=100, type="bars", resp = gsub("_", "", v[1]))

The posterior predictive check (for one of the response variable options) shows that the model predictions (\(y_{rep}\)) have grown closer to the actually observed data (y). This confirms that the model has trained well.

Evaluation

We visualize the marginal effect of each demographic factor on every response option to determine, (1) whether an option can be viewed as “common”, and (2) whether the levels of the demographic factor affect the responses to this question. First, we investigate the effect of the sector (v_1) on all response options.

conditional_effects(m, "v_1", prob = 0.95) %>% 
  purrr::imap_dfr( ~ {
    purrr::map_dfr(.x, identity) %>%
      mutate(response = str_extract(.y, "^[^.]+"))
  }) %>% 
  mutate(
    response = factor(response, levels = gsub("_", "", v), 
                      labels = labels, ordered = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = effect1__, color = effect1__)) +
    geom_point(aes(x = estimate__)) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower__, xmax = upper__)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = level.common, color = "grey", linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~response) + 
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    labs(x = "Likelihood of selecting the option", y = "Sector") + 
    guides(color = "none") +
    ggtitle(paste0("Sector affecting ", q)) +
    theme_bw()

The next figure shows the marginal effect of the project size (v_3) on the outcomes.

conditional_effects(m, "v_3", prob = 0.95) %>% 
  purrr::imap_dfr( ~ {
    purrr::map_dfr(.x, identity) %>%
      mutate(response = str_extract(.y, "^[^.]+"))
  }) %>% 
  mutate(
    response = factor(response, levels = gsub("_", "", v), 
                      labels = labels, ordered = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = effect1__)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = estimate__, color = response)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower__, ymax = upper__, fill = response), alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = level.common, color = "grey", linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~response) + 
    labs(x = "Project size", y = "Likelihood of selecting the option") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    ggtitle(paste0("Project size affecting ", q)) +
    guides(color = "none", fill = "none") +
    theme_bw()
